title: YOU’RE PROBABLY NOT AS GOOD AS YOU THINK—AND THAT MAY BE THE BEST NEWS YOU HEAR TODAY
paragraphs: YOU’RE PROBABLY NOT AS GOOD AS YOU THINK—AND THAT MAY BE THE BEST NEWS YOU HEAR TODAY

What “All Have Sinned and Fall Short” Really Says About Human Goodness—and why Romans 3 was never written merely to make bad people feel worse, but to bring every kind of person to the same place: empty-handed before Jesus Christ.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can offend a decent person faster than it can offend a criminal.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
We know the verse.
We quote it.
We put it on evangelism cards.
But sometimes we hear it as though Paul were simply saying, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
That is not nearly strong enough.
The Greek reads:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou
“For all sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
And if we allow those words to do what Paul intended them to do, they dismantle one of humanity’s favorite hiding places:
“But I’m a good person.”
Maybe you are kind.
Maybe you work hard.
Maybe you love your children.
Maybe you have never cheated on your spouse.
Maybe you give money when somebody is hurting.
Maybe you return what does not belong to you.
Maybe you have spent years helping people who could never repay you.
Those things matter.
Scripture does not require Christians to pretend that every human action is equally wicked or that unbelievers are incapable of doing things that genuinely benefit other people.

Jesus Himself spoke of sinful human beings knowing how to give good gifts to their children (Matthew 7:11). Paul wrote of Gentiles who did not possess the Mosaic Law yet sometimes did things the Law required (Romans 2:14–15).
So Christianity does not teach the ridiculous idea that every person is as cruel as he could possibly become.
Romans 3 teaches something far more unsettling.
Human goodness cannot make sinful humanity righteous before a holy God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because our favorite comparison is horizontal.
God’s standard is not.
We look sideways.
God looks perfectly.
We compare ourselves with the alcoholic.
The adulterer.
The corrupt politician.
The abusive father.
The hypocritical church leader.
The person whose scandal became public while ours remained conveniently hidden.
“I would never do what they did.”
Perhaps you wouldn't.
But Romans 3 will not permit you to make that person your measuring stick.
The standard is “the glory of God.”
τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ — tēs doxēs tou theou.
God's glory.
Not your neighbor's morality.
Not your pastor's reputation.
Not your parents' expectations.
Not society's constantly changing definition of decency.
God.
And suddenly the courtroom becomes very quiet.
Because you can outrun another sinner and still fall infinitely short of God's holiness.
Imagine two people trying to reach the stars by jumping.
One barely leaves the ground.
The other is an extraordinary athlete and leaps several feet into the air.
There is a genuine difference between their jumps.
But neither person reaches the stars.
That imperfect illustration gets us closer to Paul's devastating point.
There are meaningful moral differences between human beings. Some people live more disciplined, generous, peaceful, or outwardly honorable lives than others.
But nobody can stand before the blazing holiness of God, point to his moral résumé, and say:
“This is enough. You owe me acceptance.”
Nobody.
And that is where this verse becomes personal.
Because perhaps your greatest spiritual danger was never believing that you were evil.
Perhaps it was believing that you were good enough.
You didn't murder anyone.
But what happened inside you when someone humiliated you?
You never committed adultery.
But what have your eyes repeatedly consumed in secret?
You never robbed a bank.
But have you ever worshiped money while telling yourself you were simply being responsible?
You never abandoned your family.
But were you physically present while emotionally starving the people who needed your love?
You never publicly denied Christ.
But how many times did your silence quietly whisper, “I don't want these people to know I belong to Him”?
You worship on Sunday.
What owns your imagination on Monday?
You say, “God comes first.”
What does your calendar say?
What does your bank account say?
What does your browser history say?
What does the conversation you hope nobody ever hears say?
And deeper still...
What would happen if God exposed not merely everything you have done, but every motive underneath it?
That is where our self-defense begins to collapse.
Because sin is more than spectacular public scandal.
The Greek verb translated “sinned” is ἥμαρτον — hēmarton, from ἁμαρτάνω — hamartanō.
In Romans 3, Paul is not handing humanity a diagnosis of occasional imperfection.
He has spent the preceding chapters closing every escape route.
The openly rebellious cannot boast.
The moralist cannot boast.
The religious person cannot boast.
The Jew cannot boast in possessing the Law.
The Gentile cannot boast in ignorance of it.
Paul reaches his conclusion shortly before verse 23:
“There is none righteous, no, not one.” — Romans 3:10, KJV
Then:
“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight.” — Romans 3:20, KJV
Then comes the sentence we so often isolate:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
But please do not stop reading there.
Because stopping at Romans 3:23 can leave a sinner staring at the wound while missing the Physician standing beside him.
The sentence continues into one of the most magnificent announcements in Scripture:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24, KJV
Look at the movement.
All have sinned.
Then...
justified freely by His grace.
The Greek word translated “freely” is δωρεάν — dōrean.
Freely.
As a gift.
Without you purchasing your justification with a pile of religious accomplishments.
And “grace” is χάριτι — chariti, from χάρις — charis.
Grace.
This is where Christianity separates itself from every attempt to build a ladder into heaven out of human goodness.
The Gospel does not tell bad people to accumulate enough good deeds until God finally becomes impressed.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot justify themselves may be justified by God's grace through the redemption found in Jesus Christ.
That means the answer to your sin is not becoming slightly better than somebody else.
The answer is Christ.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because Romans 3:23 humiliates our pride...
but Romans 3:24 destroys our despair.
You are worse than your carefully edited public version suggests.
Yet in Christ there is more grace than your shame told you could possibly exist.
Read that again.
Your respectable image cannot save you.
But neither does your ugliest chapter automatically place you beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The religious person and the prostitute ultimately approach God through the same door.
The pastor and the prisoner.
The virgin and the adulterer.
The lifelong church member and the man who spent decades mocking Christianity.
The person whose sins became headlines and the person whose sins never escaped the bedroom.
Nobody enters God's kingdom carrying a certificate that says:
GOOD ENOUGH.
Those who are saved enter because of Jesus.
This is why Christianity can simultaneously destroy pride and create extraordinary hope.
At the cross, nobody gets to brag.
And nobody who comes to Christ in repentant faith gets to say His grace is insufficient.
Your goodness cannot make the cross unnecessary.
Your wickedness cannot make Christ's sufficient sacrifice inadequate.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not die merely to help basically good people become slightly nicer.
Christ died for sinners.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6, KJV
And again:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we conquered every addiction.
Not after we cleaned up our vocabulary.
Not after we restored our reputation.
Not after we became respectable enough for church people to stop whispering.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means repentance is not a payment we hand God for salvation.
Jesus began His public proclamation with the call to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15). Genuine grace does not teach us to make peace with the sin that nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your past will no longer be your master.”
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Not from scandal to pretending the scandal never happened.
Not from scandal to self-esteem.
Not from scandal to religious reputation management.
Not from scandal to “living your truth.”
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history and calling evil good.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He enters the sinner's real history with real mercy, pays for real guilt through His blood, gives real forgiveness to those who come to Him, and begins producing real transformation.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
The cross reveals how serious your sin actually is.
And then it reveals how astonishing God's grace actually is.
If sin were a minor personality defect, Calvary would be incomprehensible.
If human goodness could reconcile us to God, Christ's death would be unnecessary.
But Scripture says:
“Without shedding of blood is no remission.” — Hebrews 9:22, KJV
And Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold,
“But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” — 1 Peter 1:19, KJV
This is why boasting dies at the foot of the cross.
You cannot stand beside the crucified Son of God and congratulate yourself for being nicer than your neighbor.
Look at Him.
The crown.
The wounds.
The blood.
The rejection.
The cross.
Then try telling yourself your moral résumé was enough.
Calvary says otherwise.
But look again.
Because the cross is not merely God's indictment of human sin.
It is also God's breathtaking announcement of mercy.
The Savior knew what you were.
And He came.
He knew what humanity had become.
And He came.
He knew the betrayal.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew the disciples would run.
He knew the mockery waiting at Golgotha.
He knew every generation that would use His name casually, ignore His commandments, exploit His grace, hide behind religion, and choose darkness.
And still...
He came.
This is why Romans 3:23 should never be weaponized merely to crush somebody.
Paul's argument crushes self-righteousness so grace can become visible.
And perhaps that is what God is doing in you right now.
Maybe you clicked this because you wanted theology.
And somewhere along the way, theology started reading you.
Maybe there is something you have been defending for years.
Something you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
Pride became “standards.”
Greed became “ambition.”
Lust became “just looking.”
Bitterness became “boundaries.”
Gossip became “concern.”
Cowardice became “keeping the peace.”
Spiritual laziness became “being busy.”
Unforgiveness became “protecting myself.”
And slowly, almost invisibly, you learned how to stand near Christian language without letting Christ confront the locked rooms of your heart.
But He already knows what is behind the door.
You do not have to impress Him.
You cannot.
You do not have to deceive Him.
You cannot.
You do not have to outrun your past.
You cannot save yourself by running faster.
You need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
Maybe people ask you for prayer.
Maybe you post Scripture while privately wondering whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
Maybe the same temptation keeps returning.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then found yourself crying over the same failure.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Romans 3:23 is true about you.
But Romans 3:24 is there too.
Do not turn grace into permission to remain enslaved.
And do not turn your failures into evidence that Christ could never receive a repentant sinner like you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Run toward Christ instead of constructing another version of yourself for everyone else to admire.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice where your confidence rests.
Not in your ability to become impressive overnight.
He is faithful.
He is just.
Your hope is ultimately located outside yourself.
In Him.
That is freedom.
You can finally stop auditioning for a salvation you could never earn.
You can stop pretending another person's scandal somehow proves your innocence.
You can stop comparing stains.
You can stop hiding.
The ground beneath the cross is level.
And maybe that bothers the respectable part of us.
We want grades.
Rankings.
At least let God acknowledge that we were better than that person.
Then Jesus tells a story about a Pharisee and a tax collector.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other people.
The tax collector could barely lift his eyes.
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
Jesus said the second man went home justified.
That should haunt every religious heart that has learned to use somebody else's sin as a pedestal.
The question is not whether you can find someone worse than you.
You can.
The question is whether you are righteous enough to stand before God without Christ.
Romans answers that question.
No.
And then the Gospel answers the question you should ask next:
Can Christ save sinners who cannot save themselves?
Yes.
Completely.
That is why “all have sinned and fall short” is not ultimately a message about how worthless human beings are.
Human beings possess profound dignity because we were created in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).
Sin does not erase the fact that humanity bears God's image.
It corrupts our relationship with our Creator, disorders our loves, enslaves us, brings guilt, and leaves us unable to establish our own righteousness before God.
So Christianity gives you two truths the modern world often struggles to hold together.
You possess enormous God-given dignity.
And...
you desperately need a Savior.
You matter enormously.
And you are not your own messiah.
You were worth creating.
But your goodness cannot redeem you.
You bear God's image.
But only Christ can reconcile you to God.
That is not hatred of humanity.
That is the diagnosis that makes the cure intelligible.
A doctor who lies about the disease does not love the patient.
And a preacher who tells sinners they are already spiritually healthy when Scripture says otherwise has offered comfort at the cost of truth.
But neither should we scream the diagnosis and hide the medicine.
So hear both.
All have sinned.
And...
redemption is in Christ Jesus.
There is your scandal.
There is your grace.
There is your story.
There is mine.
And if Jesus has confronted something hidden while you have been reading this, don't perform for us.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain the entire battle publicly.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when Jesus enters the story.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who believes being “a decent person” is enough.
The believer drowning in shame.
The churchgoer who knows all the language but has never surrendered.
The son who stopped believing.
The daughter who thinks she has gone too far.
The spouse who quietly carries guilt.
The friend whose scandal has convinced them Christians will never look at them the same way again.
Or send this privately.

Sharing the Gospel is one meaningful way we can glorify God by making Christ known. Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be an act of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, faithfully, and with the right heart. Grace cannot be purchased, and giving is never a substitute for repentance, faith, obedience, prayer, love, or faithful life in Christ.
Your support helps this ministry continue the work.
They are helping carry the message farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite even the friend who does not yet believe.
Both voices are lying.
You are not saved because you were better than everybody else.
And you are not beyond salvation because your chapter became uglier than theirs.
Jesus Christ is the difference.
So when Romans says, “All have sinned,” don't rush past the mirror.
Stand there.
Let pride die.
Let excuses die.
Let comparison die.
Then keep reading.

Because immediately beyond the devastating truth that you have fallen short stands the breathtaking announcement that justification comes freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
The verse that removes your last excuse also prepares you to understand your greatest hope.
Your goodness was never strong enough to become your savior.
Your scandal was never stronger than the Savior.
And when every mask finally falls, there is still a blood-stained cross, an empty tomb, and a risen Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into life.
You spent years trying to prove you were good enough; Jesus came to give repentant sinners something infinitely better than a polished reputation—grace.
